meaning: Attached to a number + counter, it marks order: “the Nth” item, the Nth time, or the Nth day or year of a period.
connection: Number + counter + 目 (e.g. 二つ目・三番目・二回目・三年目)

senses.label: Order / position
senses.meaning: Marks the Nth item when you count in order, like English “second, third ...”. Common forms: 「〜つ目」「〜番目」「〜人目」「〜本目」.
senses.connection: Number + つ／番／人／本／杯／軒, etc. + 目
examples: Please turn right at the second corner.
I sat in the third seat from the front.
This is already my third cup of coffee.

senses.label: The Nth time
senses.meaning: Counts how many times the same thing has happened: “the Nth time”. Common forms: 「〜回目」「〜度目」.
senses.connection: Number + 回／度 + 目
examples: This is my second time coming to Japan.
I finally passed on my third try.

senses.label: The Nth day / year
senses.meaning: Counts the days or years from a starting point: “day N”, “year N”. Common forms: 「〜日目」「〜年目」「〜週目」.
senses.connection: Number + 日／年／週／か月 + 目
examples: My fever went down on my fifth day in the hospital.
This is my third year at my current company.

notes: Dropping or adding 「目」 changes the meaning completely: 「三回行きました」 means “I've been there three times” (a total), while 「三回目です」 means “this is my third time” (an order). If someone asks how many times you've been and you answer 「三回目」, you haven't answered the question.
「〜年目」 means “the Nth year”, counted from year one: 「入社三年目」 means you've actually worked there for just over two years, not “three full years” (for that, say 「入社して三年になる」).
「一番」 usually means “most” (「一番好き」 = my favorite). When listing things in order, say 「一番目」 or 「最初」; don't use plain 「一番」 as if it simply meant “the first one”.
「一日目」 (day one) is read 「いちにちめ」. Don't read it as 「ついたち」, which means the first day of the month. 「二日目」 is read 「ふつかめ」.

etymology: 「目」 originally means “eye”. It came to mean a mesh, a grid or a mark on a scale, i.e. a point or position. This is thought to have extended to a position in a sequence, giving the ordinal suffix.

similar.title: 〜(number) ＋ 助数詞 (〜本・〜人・〜枚など)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning and the most common comparison: a number + counter on its own gives a quantity (「三人来た」 = three people came); only adding 「目」 makes it an order (「三人目」 = the third person). Use the former to ask “how many / how many times” and the latter to ask “which one / which time”.

similar.title: 〜に〜回 (frequency)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning and easy to confuse: 「週に二回」 expresses frequency (twice a week), while 「二回目」 expresses order (the second time). “I go twice a week” is 「週に二回行く」; you can't add 「目」 here.

formation: 「目」 originally means “eye”, and by extension the individual marks of a mesh, grid or scale — the separate “points” along a line. A number + counter first expresses a quantity; adding 「目」 turns that quantity into “that one point” on the scale — whichever notch you've counted up to is the Nth item. So 「三人」 is a total of three people, while 「三人目」 is the person standing on the third notch. Attached to 「回・度」 it becomes “the Nth time”, and to 「日・年」 “the Nth day / year”; it's the same logic each time: turning a total into a position. And precisely because it points to “the third notch”, 「三年目」 is the third year, not three full years.

meaning: 「さ」 has two uses: attached to an adjective stem it makes a noun for degree or quality itself (高さ, 優しさ, 便利さ); and as a casual colloquial particle it can end a sentence with an easy assertion (大丈夫さ), make a challenging question, sit mid-sentence to get attention (あのさ), or report hearsay (ってさ).
connection: い-adjective / な-adjective stem + さ (nominalizing); noun, な-adjective stem, or plain form of verb / い-adjective + さ (sentence-final particle)

senses.label: Measurement / degree
senses.meaning: A measurable size or amount: 「高さ」 (height), 「長さ」 (length), 「重さ」 (weight).
senses.connection: い-adjective stem + さ (高さ・長さ・重さ・広さ・深さ・大きさ)
examples: This bridge is 500 meters long.
Please weigh the luggage.
How big is the room?

senses.label: Quality / feeling
senses.meaning: Talks about a person's character, feelings or a thing's qualities as a noun: 「優しさ」 (kindness), 「寂しさ」 (loneliness), 「美しさ」 (beauty). Often used with 「〜に感動する」 or 「〜がわかる」.
senses.connection: い-adjective stem + さ (優しさ・寂しさ・美しさ・楽しさ・よさ)
examples: I was moved by her kindness.
I finally understood how lonely it is to live alone.
The good thing about this town is that it's quiet.

senses.label: な-adjective + さ
senses.meaning: な-adjectives can also take 「さ」 to become nouns: 「便利さ」 (convenience), 「大切さ」 (importance), 「大変さ」 (difficulty). It shows the degree of that quality.
senses.connection: な-adjective stem + さ (便利さ・大切さ・大変さ・複雑さ)
examples: Everyone knows how convenient smartphones are.
When I got sick, I realized how important health is.
You won't know how hard this job is until you try it.

senses.label: Casual assertion
senses.meaning: States a conclusion lightly and offhandedly. The tone is relaxed, sometimes nonchalant or a little bit tough. Close to English “..., you know” or “sure”.
senses.connection: Noun・na-adjective stem + さ (no 「だ」); verb・i-adjective plain form + さ. Common: 「なんとかなるさ」, 「平気さ」
examples: It's fine. Things will work out.
That kind of thing? It's easy.

senses.label: Challenging question
senses.meaning: Used with a question word to push back or demand an answer with irritation. The tone is fairly sharp, like “What's so...?” or “Why do I have to...?”.
senses.connection: Question word + ... + さ／のさ. Common: 「何さ」, 「どうしてなのさ」
examples: What's so funny?
Why am I the only one getting scolded?

senses.label: Mid-sentence filler
senses.meaning: Inserted at a pause in a sentence to get the listener's attention or set the rhythm, like “so...” or “like...”. It has no real meaning. Overusing it sounds childish or sloppy.
senses.connection: Phrase・clause + さ、. Common: 「あのさ、」, 「それでさ、」
examples: Hey, can you listen to me for a sec?
So yesterday, I ran into my teacher at the station.

senses.label: Passing on hearsay
senses.meaning: 「〜ってさ」 reports what someone else said, in a light tone. Like “I heard ...” or “they say ...”.
senses.connection: Plain form + ってさ
examples: They say it's going to rain tomorrow.
I heard Tanaka is quitting the company.

notes: The noun form of 「いい」 is 「よさ」: ✕「いさ」→ ○「よさ」; likewise 「かっこいい」→「かっこよさ」.

「〜み」 attaches to only a handful of adjectives, so don't extend it by analogy: ✕「長み」「優しみ」→ ○「長さ」「優しさ」. Words that take both have different meanings: 「重さ」 is weight, 「重み」 is a sense of weight or importance.
After nouns and na-adjectives, attach 「さ」 directly with no 「だ」: ✕「学生ださ」→ ○「学生さ」.
The tone is casual and a bit nonchalant. Saying 「大丈夫さ」 or 「簡単さ」 to a boss, client or elder sounds dismissive and rude; in formal settings say 「大丈夫です」.
Dropping 「あのさ」 or 「それでさ」 into every sentence sounds childish and unsteady, especially in interviews and business talk. Use 「あの、」 or 「それで、」 instead.

etymology: The nominalizing 「さ」 is an old suffix attached to adjective stems to form nouns; 「寒さ」 and 「長さ」 already existed in Classical Japanese, and today almost every い-adjective can take it. The origin of the sentence-final 「さ」 is debated, but it is generally thought to have developed in the colloquial speech of Edo (Tokyo) in the early modern period, and it still has a casual, breezy tone.
formation: The two 「さ」 have different origins, but both are about “lightly bringing something out”. Nominalizing 「さ」: an adjective stem expresses the quality itself (「高い」 → 「高」), and 「さ」 turns it into “the degree / the quality of being ...”. This first gives a “measure” sense: 「高さ」 = height, so you can ask 「高さはどのくらい」; abstracting “degree” further gives the quality itself: 「優しさ」 is the quality of kindness. A な-adjective stem is already noun-like, so adding 「さ」 likewise gives degree (「便利さ」). The sentence-final 「さ」 attaches straight to a sentence or clause, and after nouns and な-adjectives it replaces 「だ」 (「平気さ」). It “tosses the words lightly to the listener”, neither stressing information like 「よ」 nor seeking agreement like 「ね」, so the assertion loses the hardness of 「だ」 and becomes an offhand “you know / of course”. The same casual toss at the end of a question-word sentence becomes an impatient challenge (「何さ」); inserted between clauses it only gives a pause that draws attention (「あのさ」); and after the quotative 「って」 it tosses out something one has heard, reporting hearsay (「ってさ」).

similar.title: 〜み (adjective → noun)
similar.explanation: Same kind of word formation, close in meaning: both are suffixes that turn adjectives into nouns. 「さ」 is objective and measurable (「甘さ」 = degree of sweetness), while 「み」 expresses a subjectively felt taste, depth or spot (「甘み」 = the sweetness you taste; 「言葉の重み」 = the weight of someone's words). 「み」 attaches to only a few words.

similar.title: 〜こと (nominalizer)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both can turn an adjective into a noun-like element. 「〜こと」 nominalizes the whole fact “that something is ...”, while 「〜さ」 takes only the degree of the quality: 「彼が優しいことは知っている」 (I know that he's kind) vs. 「彼の優しさに感動した」 (I was moved by his kindness).

similar.title: 〜よ
similar.explanation: Both are sentence-final and state your own judgment to the listener. 「よ」 is about clearly telling them new information; 「さ」 is more casual, with a relaxed “isn't it obvious?” feel, doesn't stress informing, and is even less suitable than 「よ」 with superiors.

similar.title: 〜ね
similar.explanation: 「ね」 seeks the listener's agreement or confirmation; with 「さ」 the speaker states a conclusion offhandedly and doesn't ask for agreement. As a mid-sentence filler, 「あのね」 is softer than 「あのさ」 and is preferred by women and when talking to children.

similar.title: 〜ぞ・〜ぜ (sentence-ending particles)
similar.explanation: Both are casual, male-leaning sentence-final assertions. 「ぞ／ぜ」 sounds firm and forceful, with a warning or rallying feel; 「さ」 comes across as light, cool, even nonchalant (「平気さ」).

meaning: Attached to adjectives of feeling or sensation, it describes how a third person feels: “shows signs of ...”, “acts like they feel ...”.
connection: い-adjective stem / な-adjective stem + がる (欲しい → 欲しがる, 嫌だ → 嫌がる)

senses.label: Other people's feelings
senses.meaning: In Japanese you can't state someone else's inner feelings as fact. 「〜がる」 describes them from the outside: “he/she seems to feel ..., shows ...”. Often used for general tendencies or habits.
senses.connection: 怖い → 怖がる／嫌だ → 嫌がる／痛い → 痛がる／寒い → 寒がる
examples: Children are afraid of shots.
My little sister really hates bugs.
Our dog is scared of the sound of thunder.

senses.label: Showing it right now
senses.meaning: 「〜がっている」 says someone is showing a feeling or desire right now. It's more concrete and immediate than 「〜がる」.
senses.connection: 欲しい → 欲しがっている／寂しい → 寂しがっている／残念だ → 残念がっている
examples: My little brother really wants the new game.
My daughter, who's studying abroad, is feeling lonely.
We lost the match, and everyone was disappointed.

senses.label: Putting on an act
senses.meaning: 「強がる」, 「面白がる」 and similar verbs mean deliberately acting a certain way: “act tough”, “do something for the fun of it”.
senses.connection: 強い → 強がる／面白い → 面白がる
examples: He's actually scared, but he's acting tough.
The kids thought it was funny and pressed it over and over.

notes: 「〜がる」 turns the expression into a transitive godan verb, so the object particle changes from 「が」 to 「を」: ✕「弟は犬が怖がる」→ ○「弟は犬を怖がる」; ✕「水が欲しがる」→ ○「水を欲しがる」.
For your own feelings, use the adjective directly: ✕「私は寂しがっています」→ ○「私は寂しいです」. Using it about yourself sounds as if you were coldly describing someone else, which is very unnatural.
Used about superiors, elders or clients, it suggests they are “acting like a child”, which is rude: ✕「部長が欲しがっていました」→ ○「部長が欲しいとおっしゃっていました」.
The verb form of 「嫌だ」 is 「嫌がる」: ✕「嫌いがる」→ ○「嫌がる」. 「人の嫌がることをしない」 (don't do what others dislike) is a common piece of advice.

etymology: 「がる」 is thought to come from an old suffix meaning “to show signs of ..., to act like ...”. Classical Japanese already had forms like 「ゆかしがる」 and 「をかしがる」, and it later became a fixed suffix that turns adjectives of feeling into verbs.

similar.title: 〜たがる
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「たい」 + 「がる」, showing outwardly a wish to do something. This pattern attaches to adjectives (「怖がる」「欲しがる」), while 「〜たがる」 attaches to the verb masu-stem (「行きたがる」): wanting a thing is 「欲しがる」, wanting to do an action is 「〜たがる」.

similar.title: 〜がり (〜がり屋)
similar.explanation: Same origin: the noun made from the stem of 「がる」, meaning “a person with that tendency”: 「寒がり」 = someone who feels the cold easily, 「怖がり」 = a scaredy-cat. 「〜がる」 describes a single display or tendency, while 「〜がり」 directly labels someone's personality.

similar.title: 〜そうだ (appearance)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both infer someone's feelings from how they look. 「寂しそうだ」 is the speaker's judgment that someone “looks lonely”; 「寂しがっている」 means the person is actually showing loneliness in words or behavior (e.g. keeps saying they want to go home). When you're not sure, 「〜そうだ」 is the safer choice.

similar.title: 〜がほしい
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: 「〜がほしい」 states what you yourself want (「私は新しい靴がほしい」). For what someone else wants, change it to 「〜を欲しがっている」, and the particle switches from 「が」 to 「を」 as well.

formation: The adjective stem expresses an inner feeling or sensation (「怖」「寂し」「欲し」), and it's followed by the suffix 「がる」, meaning “to show signs of ..., to behave that way”. Together they mean “to show that feeling on the outside”. In Japanese you can't state outright what's going on inside another person; you can only describe what's visible, so 「〜がる」 is naturally used for third persons. 「がる」 turns the adjective into a godan verb, so it can take an object with 「を」 and use 「〜ている」 for a state that's showing right now. What shows on the outside can also be put on deliberately, which gives words like 「強がる」 (to put on a brave face) and 「面白がる」 (to make a show of finding something funny).

meaning: Describes a third person's wish to do something. It's how 「〜たい」 is used for other people.
connection: Verb ます-stem + たがる (行きます → 行きたがる)

senses.label: Others want to do
senses.meaning: From someone's words or behavior, you can see they want to do something. The speaker observes and describes it from the outside. 「〜たがっている」 is common for a current state.
senses.connection: Verb ます-stem + たがる／たがっている
examples: Kids always want to play outside.
My little brother wants to buy a new smartphone.
The cat wants to go outside.

senses.label: Not wanting to
senses.meaning: The negative 「〜たがらない」 means someone doesn't want to or won't do something. Often used for children, pets or people in general.
senses.connection: Verb ます-stem + たがらない
examples: My son won't eat his vegetables.
He doesn't like talking about the past.

senses.label: General tendency
senses.meaning: 「〜たがるものだ」 says people in general have this wish or tendency.
senses.connection: Verb ます-stem + たがるものだ／たがる人が多い
examples: People like to talk about themselves.
Young people want to live in big cities.

notes: Use it only for third persons; for yourself, use 「〜たい」: ✕「私は日本へ行きたがっています」→ ○「私は日本へ行きたいです」.
Before 「〜たい」 you can use 「が」 or 「を」, but 「〜たがる」 takes only 「を」: ✕「弟は水が飲みたがる」→ ○「弟は水を飲みたがる」.
「〜たがる」 carries a judgmental nuance of “keeps wanting to, makes a fuss about wanting to”, so using it about superiors or clients is rude: ✕「部長が会いたがっています」→ ○「部長が会いたいとおっしゃっています」.
Likewise, don't ask a superior directly about their wishes (“Would you like to ...?”): ✕「先生、コーヒーを飲みたいですか」→ ○「先生、コーヒーはいかがですか」.

etymology: It combines 「た」, the stem of the wish auxiliary 「たい」, with the suffix 「がる」 (“show signs of”). Literally “show signs of wanting to”, so it describes someone else's wish as seen from the outside.

similar.title: 〜たい
similar.explanation: Same origin: the first half of 「〜たがる」 is 「たい」. 「〜たい」 expresses your own wish (「私は帰りたい」); for someone else, change it to 「〜たがっている」 or report it with 「〜たいそうだ」「〜たいと言っている」.

similar.title: 〜がる・〜がっている
similar.explanation: Same origin: both use 「がる」 to show a feeling outwardly. 「〜がる」 attaches to adjectives (「欲しがる」「怖がる」), and 「〜たがる」 to the verb masu-stem (「遊びたがる」).

similar.title: 〜てほしい・〜てもらいたい
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both express a wish. 「〜たがる」 is a third person wanting to do something themselves; 「〜てほしい」 is the speaker wanting someone else to do something: 「子供は外で遊びたがる」 (the kids want to play outside) vs. 「子供に外で遊んでほしい」 (I want the kids to play outside).

formation: 「たい」 expresses the speaker's own inner wish, and 「がる」 means “to show a feeling on the outside”. Put together = “to show outwardly a wish to do something”: the speaker is describing words and actions observed from outside rather than declaring what's in the other person's mind, which is why it's used for third persons. Because it's a wish that's on display for anyone to see, it often sounds like “keeps wanting to, makes a fuss about it”, which is why it comes across as rude about superiors. 「がる」 turns the whole thing into a godan verb, so the object can only take 「を」, and the negative 「〜たがらない」 means “shows no wish to”.

meaning: Attached to a verb's ます-stem, it shows that an action or change begins: “start to ...”, “begin ...ing”.
connection: Verb ます-stem + 始める (読みます → 読み始める)

senses.label: Starting to do
senses.meaning: A deliberate action begins: “start ...ing”. It only marks the starting point; the action goes on afterward.
senses.connection: Volitional verb ます-stem + 始める (読み始める・習い始める・使い始める)
examples: I started learning the piano last year.
I only started reading this book yesterday.
OK everyone, let's start eating.

senses.label: A change begins
senses.meaning: A natural phenomenon or change of state starts to appear. Often used with 「少しずつ」 or 「だんだん」.
senses.connection: Non-volitional verb ます-stem + 始める (降り始める・咲き始める・わかり始める)
examples: It started to rain.
The cherry blossoms in the park have started to bloom.
Lately I've slowly started to understand Japanese.

notes: Whether the first verb is intransitive or transitive, the second part is always the transitive 「始める」: ✕「雨が降り始まった」→ ○「雨が降り始めた」.
「〜始める」 can be used for invitations, requests and intentions, but 「〜出す」 can't: ✕「では、書き出してください」→ ○「では、書き始めてください」.
It attaches to the masu-stem, not the te-form: ✕「勉強して始める」→ ○「勉強し始める」 (or 「勉強を始める」).
Instantaneous verbs generally can't take it: ✕「電車が駅に着き始めた」. It only works when the subject is plural and the sense is “one after another”: 「お客さんが集まり始めた」.

etymology: 「始める」 means “to start (something)” and is the transitive partner of 「始まる」. As the second part of a compound verb after a ます-stem, it marks the beginning stage of the first action.

similar.title: 〜出す
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both express a start. 「〜出す」 stresses that it's sudden or unexpected and can't be used for intentions or requests; 「〜始める」 is a neutral start, so you can say 「読み始めましょう」. 「急に泣き出した」 sounds more sudden than 「泣き始めた」.

similar.title: 〜てくる
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: when a change begins, the two are often interchangeable, but 「〜てくる」 carries a felt sense of the change “coming toward you”: 「雨が降ってきた」 (it's started raining); 「雨が降り始めた」 just states objectively that the rain began.

similar.title: 〜かける・〜かけの
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both concern the beginning of an action. With 「〜始める」, the action continues once started; 「〜かける」 means it was just begun and then stopped, or is about to happen: 「読みかけの本」 (a half-read book), 「言いかけてやめた」 (started to say something and stopped).

similar.title: 〜をはじめ
similar.explanation: Same origin: both come from 「始める」. 「〜をはじめ」 presents something as “the leading example at the top of the list”: 「東京をはじめ、大阪や名古屋でも」. The meaning has shifted from “starting an action” to “first and foremost, led by ...”.

formation: 「始める」 is the transitive verb “to start (something)”. Attached to the verb masu-stem (連用形), it forms a compound verb: the first part says what you do, and 「始める」 pins down the starting point of that action. Since the second part is only about the beginning, the sentence is about entering the phase of that action, so the first verb needs to be an action that can continue — once started, it goes on. 「始める」 itself is something you can do on purpose, so the whole compound can take volitional and request forms like 「〜ましょう」「〜てください」. Even when the first verb describes a natural phenomenon (「降る」「咲く」), the second part stays 「始める」: as the second element of a compound it has become grammaticalized and no longer switches to intransitive 「始まる」.

meaning: Attached to a verb's ます-stem, it shows an action starting suddenly, or means “out” (taking something out, bringing something to light).
connection: Verb ます-stem + 出す (泣きます → 泣き出す)

senses.label: Sudden start
senses.meaning: An action or phenomenon starts suddenly or unexpectedly: “burst into ...”, “suddenly start ...ing”. Often used with 「急に」 or 「突然」.
senses.connection: Verb ます-stem + 出す (泣き出す・降り出す・笑い出す・走り出す)
examples: It suddenly started raining.
The baby burst into tears.
When they heard that, everyone burst out laughing.

senses.label: Starting to move
senses.meaning: Something that was still starts to move or run.
senses.connection: 動き出す・歩き出す・走り出す, etc.
examples: The doors closed, and the train started moving.
My one-year-old daughter has finally started walking.

senses.label: Out / to light
senses.meaning: Taking something out, or bringing something hidden to the surface. Many of these compounds have become words of their own.
senses.connection: 取り出す・飛び出す・思い出す・見つけ出す・呼び出す, etc.
examples: I took my wallet out of my bag.
I remembered things from the past.
The cat suddenly dashed out of the room.

notes: It can't be used for intentions, invitations, requests or commands: ✕「明日から日記を書き出そう」→ ○「明日から日記を書き始めよう」.
「思い出す」「取り出す」「言い出す」 and similar words have become set vocabulary meaning “remember, take out, bring up”, not “start to think, start to take”: 「名前を思い出した」 = I remembered the name.
It attaches to the masu-stem, not the te-form: ✕「泣いて出した」→ ○「泣き出した」.
Using it for a planned start of your own sounds as if even you didn't see it coming: for starting work or school as scheduled, use 「〜始める」 — 「九時から作業を始めた」, not 「作業し出した」.

daily.title: With children
daily.description: Explaining to your family why your little brother is crying.
daily.example: His toy got taken, and my little brother started crying.

daily.title: Sudden rain
daily.description: You and a friend get caught in the rain at the park.
daily.example: The sky got dark, and it started to rain.

daily.title: Remembering an appointment
daily.description: You suddenly remember a plan.
daily.example: Oh! I just remembered I have a dentist appointment today.

work.title: Project launch
work.description: Saying in a meeting that a plan is finally underway.
work.example: The new project has finally gotten moving.

work.title: Organizing documents
work.description: Taking files out of a cabinet.
work.example: Please take last year's documents off the shelf.

etymology: 「出す」 originally means “to put out, take out”. As the second part of a compound verb, it first meant “take outward” (取り出す), then extended to “make an action appear”, i.e. to start suddenly.

similar.title: 〜始める
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both express a start. 「〜始める」 is neutral and works for intentions and requests; 「〜出す」 stresses something sudden and uncontrollable: 「赤ちゃんが急に泣き出した」 is perfectly natural, but you can't say 「さあ、食べ出しましょう」.

similar.title: 〜てくる
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both work when a phenomenon starts to appear. 「雨が降ってきた」 stresses the change gradually reaching you, 「雨が降り出した」 a sudden start. When you gradually get hungry, say 「お腹が空いてきた」, not 「空き出した」.

similar.title: 〜かける・〜かけの
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both concern the beginning of an action. With 「〜出す」 the action carries on after it starts; with 「〜かける」 it's begun and then stopped: 「言い出した」 (came out and said it) vs. 「言いかけた」 (was about to say it but held back).

formation: 「出す」 originally means “to bring from inside to outside”. As the second part of a compound verb, it first kept the concrete sense of “taking out, letting out”: 「取り出す」「飛び出す」. Shift “coming out” from space to time and you get an action emerging and appearing out of a state of “nothing” — in other words, starting. “Bursting out” is usually instantaneous and uncontrolled, so 「〜出す」 carries a nuance of “suddenly, unexpectedly”, and for the same reason it can't be used for planned intentions or requests. Some 「〜出す」 compounds kept the spatial meaning and became words in their own right (「思い出す」 = to take a memory out), so you need to tell “starting” apart from “outward”.

meaning: Attached to a verb's ます-stem, it means finishing an action: “finish ...ing”.
connection: Verb ます-stem + 終わる／終える (読みます → 読み終わる)

senses.label: Finishing
senses.meaning: An action that takes some time is completed. It just states the fact, with no emotional nuance.
senses.connection: Durative verb ます-stem + 終わる (読み終わる・食べ終わる・書き終わる)
examples: When you finish reading this book, please lend it to me.
I've finished eating dinner.
I can't go to bed until I finish writing the report.

senses.label: 〜終える
senses.meaning: 「〜終える」 means basically the same as 「〜終わる」 but is more formal. It's common in formal situations and in writing.
senses.connection: Verb ます-stem + 終える (読み終える・使い終える)
examples: Everyone has finished taking the exam.
When you're done with the dishes, please put them back on the shelf.

notes: It only attaches to actions that have duration; instantaneous verbs can't take it: ✕「駅に着き終わった」→ ○「駅に着いた」.
「終わる」 itself is intransitive, but in the compound the object still follows the first verb and takes 「を」: ✕「本が読み終わった」→ ○「本を読み終わった」.
It attaches to the masu-stem, not the te-form: ✕「食べて終わった」→ ○「食べ終わった」.

「〜終わる」 simply means “finished doing” objectively, with no regret: 「お金を使い終わった」 (I've used up that money — neutral) vs. 「お金を使ってしまった」 (I went and spent the money — regret). Don't use 「〜終わる」 when you mean “did it by mistake”.

daily.title: Family meal
daily.description: A child finishes eating and asks to go play.
daily.example: Can I go out and play when I finish eating?

daily.title: Borrowing a book
daily.description: A friend asks when you'll return the book.
daily.example: I'll give it back as soon as I finish reading it.

daily.title: Washing machine
daily.description: Letting your family know the washing machine is free.
daily.example: I'm done with the washing machine.

work.title: Checking progress
work.description: Reporting to your boss that the data entry is done.
work.example: I've finished entering all the data.

work.title: Meeting room rules
work.description: A line from a company notice.
work.example: Please turn off the lights when you finish using the meeting room.

etymology: 「終わる」 means “to end”. As the second part of a compound verb after a ます-stem, it shows the first action reaching its end. 「終える」 is the transitive partner and sounds more formal.

similar.title: 〜てしまう
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both can express completion. 「〜終わる」 just means objectively finishing; 「〜てしまう」 often adds regret on top of completion: 「レポートを書き終わった」 (I finished writing the report) vs. 「大事な書類を捨ててしまった」 (I accidentally threw away an important document).

similar.title: 〜切る
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both mean doing something to the end. 「〜切る」 stresses “all of it, completely, nothing left”: 「マラソンを走り切った」 (ran the whole marathon), 「お金を使い切った」 (spent every last yen); 「〜終わる」 only says the action ended.

similar.title: 〜抜く
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: 「〜抜く」 means overcoming difficulties and sticking with it to the end: 「最後まで戦い抜いた」, with a sense of perseverance and effort; 「〜終わる」 is just a neutral “finished doing”.

formation: 「終わる」 means “to end”. As the second part of a compound attached to the verb masu-stem, it marks the end point of the first action: 「読み終わる」 = to read to the end. Because it's about the end of a process, the first verb has to be an action with a process and some length; something over in an instant, like 「着く」 or 「死ぬ」, has no process to finish. The object is determined by the first verb (「本を読む」→「本を読み終わる」), so even though 「終わる」 is intransitive, the compound still uses 「を」. The corresponding transitive verb 「終える」 means “to bring to an end deliberately”, so 「〜終える」 sounds like a conscious completion and is more formal.

meaning: Attached to a verb's ます-stem, it shows an action going on without stopping: “keep ...ing”, “continue to ...”.
connection: Verb ます-stem + 続ける (歩きます → 歩き続ける)

senses.label: Keep on doing
senses.meaning: Doing an action nonstop over a period of time. Often used with words for a length of time like 「ずっと」, 「〜時間」 or 「〜年間」.
senses.connection: Verb ます-stem + 続ける (歩き続ける・待ち続ける・働き続ける)
examples: I kept walking for three hours to get to the station.
He has been working at the same company for ten years.
I kept waiting for an hour, but he never came.

senses.label: Sticking with it
senses.meaning: Deliberately keeping something up without giving up or stopping. Often used with 「これからも」 or 「あきらめずに」.
senses.connection: Volitional verb ます-stem + 続ける／続けたい／続けよう
examples: I want to keep studying Japanese from now on, too.
I've kept a diary ever since I was a child.

notes: Deliberate human actions must use 「〜続ける」: ✕「三時間歩き続いた」→ ○「三時間歩き続けた」. Intransitive 「〜続く」 is limited to a few natural phenomena such as 「降り続く」「鳴り続く」.
「〜ている」 only says something is going on; 「〜続けている」 stresses that it hasn't stopped: “I'm eating” is 「食べている」, while 「食べ続けている」 means “I keep eating nonstop”.
With instantaneous verbs, 「〜続ける」 can only mean repetition: 「ドアをたたき続ける」 = to keep knocking on the door; ✕「死に続ける」 doesn't work.
It attaches to the masu-stem, not the te-form: ✕「勉強して続ける」→ ○「勉強し続ける」.

daily.title: Talking about hobbies
daily.description: Telling a friend about something you've done for years.
daily.example: I've been playing the piano since I was five.

daily.title: Waiting for someone
daily.description: Your friend was very late, and you complain about it.
daily.example: I waited a whole hour in the cold!

daily.title: Encouraging a friend
daily.description: A friend wants to give up running, and you cheer them on.
daily.example: If you keep running a little every day, you'll definitely get faster.

work.title: Company speech
work.description: The president talks about company policy at the year-end party.
work.example: We will continue to make good products for our customers.

work.title: News report
work.description: A report on rising prices.
work.example: Prices keep going up.

etymology: 「続ける」 is the transitive partner of 「続く」 (to continue) and means “to keep something going”. As the second part of a compound verb, it shows the first action going on without a break.

similar.title: 〜ていく
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: 「〜ていく」 expresses carrying on from now into the future, often with determination: 「これからも勉強していきたい」; 「〜続ける」 stresses not stopping along the way: 「勉強し続けたい」.

similar.title: 〜ている
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: 「〜ている」 only says an action is in progress; 「〜続けている」 stresses a long stretch without stopping: 「雨が降っている」 (it's raining) vs. 「雨が三日も降り続けている」 (it's been raining for three days straight).

similar.title: 〜っぱなし
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both involve continuation. 「〜っぱなし」 means leaving a state as it is and often shows annoyance: 「電気をつけっぱなし」「一日中立ちっぱなし」; 「〜続ける」 means actively keeping on doing the action, and can be positive or negative.

similar.title: 〜抜く
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: 「〜抜く」 means seeing something difficult through to the end: 「最後まで走り抜いた」; 「〜続ける」 only says you kept doing it, without saying whether you reached the end.

formation: 「続ける」 is the transitive form of 「続く」 (to continue), meaning “to keep something going without a break”. Attached to the verb masu-stem, it means “to keep this action going without a break”. Because the focus is on there being no break in between, it often pairs with durations like 「三時間」「十年間」, and with a deliberate subject it becomes “to persist”. If the first verb is over in an instant, “no break” can only be understood as the same action happening again and again — repetition.

meaning: Shows movement toward the speaker, going somewhere to do something and coming back, a change starting to appear, or something continuing from the past up to now.

senses.label: Coming this way
senses.meaning: A person or thing moves toward the speaker: “come ...ing”, “come in”.
senses.connection: Movement verb te-form + くる (走ってくる・入ってくる・持ってくる)
examples: A child came running toward us from over there.
A bird flew in through the window.
My older brother brought a big box.

senses.label: Go and come back
senses.meaning: Going somewhere, doing something, then coming back. 「行ってきます」 is the set phrase you say when leaving home.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + くる (行ってくる・買ってくる・見てくる)
examples: I'm just popping out to the convenience store.
I bought the tickets at the station (and came back).
I'll go grab lunch first.

senses.label: A change appears
senses.meaning: A change starts and gradually becomes noticeable: “getting ...”, “start to ...”. Often used with 「だんだん」 or 「急に」.
senses.connection: Change verb te-form + くる (なってくる・降ってくる・空いてくる)
examples: It's started to rain.
It's gradually getting colder, isn't it?
I'm getting hungry.

senses.label: Up to now
senses.meaning: An action has continued from the past up to now: “have been ...ing all along”. Often used with 「今まで」 or 「〜年間」.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + きた (住んできた・頑張ってきた)
examples: I've lived in this town for twenty years.
I've worked really hard up to now.

senses.label: Directed at me
senses.meaning: Someone else's action is aimed at the speaker.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + くる (電話をかけてくる・話しかけてくる・送ってくる)
examples: A friend called me in the middle of the night.
A stranger came up and spoke to me.

notes: 「〜てきた」 covers the period from the past up to now, so it can't go with 「これから」: ✕「これからも頑張ってきます」→ ○「これからも頑張っていきます」.
Get the direction wrong and the meaning flips: 「兄が本を持ってきた」 (brought it here) vs. 「兄が本を持っていった」 (took it away).
「〜てくる」 and 「〜てくれる」 differ by just one sound: 「知らない人が話しかけてきた」 only shows direction and is often used for unwelcome actions; 「話しかけてくれた」 turns it into “they kindly spoke to me”, with gratitude.
「くる」 conjugates like 「来る」: ✕「帰ってきない」→ ○「帰ってこない」; the potential form is 「〜てこられる」.

daily.title: Leaving home
daily.description: Said to your family as you head out.
daily.example: I'm off! (lit. “I'll go and come back.”)

daily.title: Talking about the weather
daily.description: Chatting with a neighbor about the season.
daily.example: It's been getting warmer lately, hasn't it?

daily.title: Asking a favor
daily.description: Asking a family member to pick something up on the way home.
daily.example: Buy some milk on your way home.

work.title: Leaving your desk
work.description: Letting coworkers know you're stepping out.
work.example: I'm going to the post office. I'll be back in about thirty minutes.

work.title: Job interview
work.description: Describing your work history in an interview.
work.example: I've worked in sales for the past five years.

work.title: Message from a client
work.description: Telling your boss a client got in touch.
work.example: Company A sent us a quote a little while ago.

etymology: It's a verb te-form plus 「来る」 (come). It first meant spatial movement “toward the speaker”, then extended to time: “from the past up to now” and “a change arriving in front of you”.

similar.title: 〜ていく
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: a pair with the same structure and opposite directions, and the comparison learners see most. In space, 「持ってくる」 (bring) vs. 「持っていく」 (take); in time, 「〜てきた」 is up to now and 「〜ていく」 is from now on: 「今まで頑張ってきた。これからも頑張っていく」.

similar.title: 〜始める
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: when a change begins, 「降ってきた」 conveys a felt sense of it happening around the speaker, while 「降り始めた」 objectively states the starting point.

similar.title: 〜に行く・〜に来る (purpose)
similar.explanation: Same origin: both use 「来る」. 「買いに来る」 is “come in order to buy” (purpose); 「買ってくる」 is “go buy and come back” (do first, then return): 「ちょっとジュースを買ってくるね」.

similar.title: 〜てくれる
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both work when an action is directed at me, but 「〜てくれる」 adds gratitude while 「〜てくる」 only shows direction: 「友達が手伝ってくれた」 (grateful) vs. 「友達が夜中に電話をかけてきた」 (neutral or annoyed).

formation: 「て」 links the preceding action to 「来る」 as one unit, and 「来る」 means “to come toward the speaker”. In space, the action comes with movement toward me → 「走ってくる」; or you go do something and then return to my side → 「買ってくる」. Replace “my side” with “now” and you get, in time, “coming all the way from the past to the present” → 「住んできた」. Apply “arriving in front of me” to a change, and the change appears before the speaker → 「寒くなってきた」. Someone else's action aimed at my side gives 「電話をかけてきた」. All five senses revolve around one core: approaching the speaker's here and now.

meaning: Shows movement away from the speaker, doing something before leaving, or a change or action continuing from now into the future.

senses.label: Moving away
senses.meaning: A person or thing moves away from the speaker: “go ...ing”, “go off”.
senses.connection: Movement verb te-form + いく (飛んでいく・帰っていく・持っていく)
examples: The bird flew off into the sky.
The children ran off home.
Please take an umbrella with you tomorrow.

senses.label: Changing from now on
senses.meaning: A change develops from now into the future: “more and more”, “keep ...ing”. Often used with 「これから」 or 「どんどん」.
senses.connection: Change verb te-form + いく (なっていく・減っていく・増えていく)
examples: It's going to get colder and colder from now on.
This town's population will probably keep shrinking.
I think I'll gradually get used to my new life.

senses.label: Keep doing from now on
senses.meaning: Continuing an action from now on. It often expresses resolve or plans.
senses.connection: Volitional verb te-form + いきたい／いこう／いきます
examples: I want to keep studying Japanese from now on.
Let's join forces and build our life together, the two of us.

senses.label: Do before leaving
senses.meaning: Doing something before you leave: “... before you go”.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + いく (飲んでいく・寄っていく・食べていく)
examples: We have time, so let's have some tea before we go.
Why don't you stop by my place on your way home?

notes: 「〜ていく」 runs from now into the future, so it can't describe experience up to now: ✕「十年間日本語を勉強していきました」→ ○「十年間日本語を勉強してきました」.
Reverse the direction and the meaning reverses: 「傘を持っていく」 (take it with you) vs. 「傘を持ってくる」 (bring it here). Judge from where the speaker is: taking it away from me is 「いく」, bringing it to me is 「くる」.
「いく」 conjugates like 「行く」, and the past is 「〜ていった」: ✕「持っていいた」→ ○「持っていった」.
The spoken contractions 「〜てく」「〜てった」 are very casual; with superiors, clients or in formal settings, use the full 「〜ていきます」.

daily.title: Reminder before going out
daily.description: A mother reminds her child to take something.
daily.example: It looks like rain, so take an umbrella with you.

daily.title: When a friend visits
daily.description: You ask a visiting friend to eat before leaving.
daily.example: Since you're here, stay and have dinner before you go.

daily.title: Talking about the future
daily.description: Chatting with a friend about your plans.
daily.example: From now on, I'm going to walk every day for my health.

work.title: Business policy
work.description: The president talks about the company's direction in a meeting.
work.example: We will keep expanding our business overseas.

work.title: News commentary
work.description: A news program predicts changes in society.
work.example: The number of elderly people is expected to keep rising.

etymology: It's a verb te-form plus 「行く」 (go). It first meant spatial movement “away from here”, then extended to time: “moving forward from now into the future”.

similar.title: 〜てくる
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: a pair with the same structure and opposite directions. 「〜ていく」 moves away from my side and toward the future; 「〜てくる」 moves toward my side and arrives at the present: 「これまで頑張ってきた。これからも頑張っていく」.

similar.title: 〜続ける
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: 「〜ていく」 expresses carrying on from now on, often with determination; 「〜続ける」 stresses not stopping along the way: 「これからも勉強していきます」 vs. 「三時間勉強し続けた」.

similar.title: 〜に行く・〜に来る (purpose)
similar.explanation: Same origin: both use 「行く」. 「買いに行く」 is “go in order to buy”; 「買っていく」 is “buy and then go / buy and take with you”: 「お土産を買っていこう」.

formation: 「て」 links the preceding action to 「行く」, and 「行く」 means “to leave the speaker's place and go off into the distance”. In space, the action comes with moving away → 「飛んでいった」; or you do something before you leave → 「お茶を飲んでいこう」 (let's have some tea before we go). Replace “here” with “now” and you get, in time, “moving forward from now into the future” → 「寒くなっていく」「勉強していきたい」. So the core of 「〜ていく」 is “setting out from the speaker's here and now, outward and onward”, the exact counterpart of 「〜てくる」, “approaching the here and now”.

meaning: Expresses a sound, smell or taste you perceive with your senses, or a physical or mental feeling.
connection: Nouns like 音／声／匂い／味／香り／気 + がする

senses.label: Sounds
senses.meaning: A sound is heard: “there's a sound of ...”, “I hear ...”. The sound reaches you on its own; you're not deliberately listening.
senses.connection: 音／声／物音 + がする
examples: There's a strange noise coming from the next room.
I heard a child's voice outside.

senses.label: Smells / tastes
senses.meaning: A smell or taste is perceived: “it smells / tastes ...”. Often used with modifiers like 「いい」, 「変な」 or 「〜のような」.
senses.connection: 匂い／臭い／香り／味 + がする
examples: Something smells good in the kitchen.
This soup has an unusual taste.
When I walked into the room, I smelled flowers.

senses.label: Physical / mental feelings
senses.meaning: A physical discomfort, or a vague feeling or hunch. 「〜気がする」 means “I have a feeling that ...”.
senses.connection: 気／寒気／吐き気／頭痛／感じ + がする
examples: I have a feeling something good is going to happen today.
I've had a headache since this morning.
I felt a chill, so I took my temperature.

notes: 「声がする」 means “I hear a voice”, not that you yourself make a sound: ✕「もっと大きい声がしてください」→ ○「もっと大きい声を出してください」.
「〜がする」 means “to perceive”, while 「〜をしている」 means “to have a certain feature”: 「台所からいい匂いがする」 (I smell something good from the kitchen) vs. 「この花はいい匂いをしている」 (this flower itself smells nice).
Body parts can't go directly before it: ✕「頭がする」→ ○「頭痛がする」「頭が痛い」.
「〜気がする」 is even less certain than 「〜と思う」. Leaning on it when giving your judgment to a superior or client at work sounds vague and evasive; when a clear opinion is needed, say 「〜と思います」「〜と考えます」.

etymology: 「する」 originally had a broad meaning and could express that a phenomenon occurs or exists. The 「する」 in 「音がする」 and 「匂いがする」 is this use: a sensation “arises, is present”.

similar.title: 〜ような気がする
similar.explanation: Same origin: an extended form of 「気がする」. Adding 「〜ような」 makes the judgment softer and less certain: 「どこかで会ったような気がする」.

similar.title: 〜が見える・〜が聞こえる
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both express perceiving something naturally. 「音が聞こえる」 focuses on your ears being able to hear it (you can say 「聞こえない」); 「音がする」 focuses on a sound being there. Sight has no 「〜がする」 form; use 「〜が見える」.

similar.title: 〜と思う (I think)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: 「〜気がする」 is less certain and more gut-based than 「〜と思う」: 「明日は雨だと思う」 involves some judgment, while 「明日は雨が降る気がする」 is just a vague feeling.

formation: At its most basic, 「する」 has a very broad meaning: besides “to do”, it can mean that some phenomenon appears or exists. In 「noun + が + する」, 「が」 marks the sensation itself (a sound, smell, taste or feeling) as the subject, and 「する」 says that it has arisen. So 「音がする」 literally means “a sound occurs”; the speaker merely perceives it passively, with no sense of “doing”. Replace the sensation with 「気」 (mind, feeling) and you get 「気がする」 = a feeling arises in your mind → “I have a feeling that ...”. Precisely because the subject is the sensation itself, a person can't go in the 「が」 slot, and it can't be changed to 「を」.

meaning: Shows that a state stays as it is, or that you do something while that state continues: “with ... still ...”, “as it is”.
connection: Verb た-form / ない-form + まま; い-adjective + まま; な-adjective + な / noun + の + まま

senses.label: Doing something in that state
senses.meaning: 「〜たまま」 means doing the next action while the previous state is unchanged. The second part is often something that shouldn't be done that way, so it sounds odd or improper.
senses.connection: Verb た-form + まま (つけたまま・履いたまま・開けたまま)
examples: Please don't come into the room with your shoes on.
I fell asleep with the light on.
I went out with the window open.

senses.label: Nothing has changed
senses.meaning: 「〜ままだ」 and 「〜ままになっている」 mean a state has stayed the same, and a change that should have happened hasn't.
senses.connection: Verb た-form / ない-form, or noun + の + ままだ
examples: The desk is just as it was yesterday.
I still haven't returned the book I borrowed.
This town is just the way it used to be.

senses.label: As it is
senses.meaning: 「そのまま」 and 「このまま」 mean leaving something as it is, without changing it: “just like this”, “as is”.
senses.connection: この／その／あの + まま
examples: It's fine like this.
You can eat this vegetable as it is, without cooking.
Please keep going straight ahead.

notes: 「靴を履いて入った」 only gives the order of events, while 「靴を履いたまま入った」 stresses “went in without taking your shoes off”. In Japan, walking into a home or a tatami room with your shoes on is a serious breach of manners, and you'll often see the sign 「靴のまま上がらないでください」.
Use the た-form before it for a state that's already in place: ✕「電気をつけるまま寝た」→ ○「電気をつけたまま寝た」.
For doing two things at the same time, use 「〜ながら」, not 「〜たまま」: ✕「音楽を聞いたまま勉強する」→ ○「音楽を聞きながら勉強する」. 「〜たまま」 only goes with states that are kept up, like “wearing, left on, standing”.
「まま」 is a noun, so nouns take 「の」 and な-adjectives take 「な」: ✕「昔まま」→ ○「昔のまま」; ✕「きれいまま」→ ○「きれいなまま」.

etymology: 「まま」 is written 「儘」 in kanji and originally meant “as it is, as one wishes”. In older Japanese, 「心のまま」 meant “as one pleases”. Today it's mostly written in kana and means “keeping the original state”.

similar.title: 〜っぱなし
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both express a state continuing. 「〜っぱなし」 focuses on leaving things be and not finishing what should be finished; it's more colloquial and often shows annoyance: 「窓を開けっぱなしにする」. 「〜たまま」 can describe things purely objectively: 「窓を開けたまま寝た」.

similar.title: 〜ないで (without doing)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: the same event can be described from two sides: 「靴を脱がないで入った」 (without taking shoes off) = 「靴を履いたまま入った」 (with shoes on). 「〜ないで」 says what you didn't do; 「〜たまま」 says what state was kept.

similar.title: 〜ままに (as one pleases / as told)
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「まま」 + 「に」 means “letting ... guide you, just as ...”: 「足の向くままに歩く」 (wander wherever your feet take you), 「言われるままにサインした」 (signed just as I was told). This pattern keeps a state unchanged; 「〜ままに」 means going along with someone's will or instructions.

similar.title: 〜たなり (state left unchanged)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning (written): 「〜たなり」 also means that after doing something, things stayed that way and what should have happened didn't: 「出かけたなり帰ってこない」. It's more literary and old-fashioned than 「〜たまま」.

formation: 「まま」 is a formal noun meaning “as is, unchanged” (written 「儘」 in kanji). The modifier in front of it tells you which “as is”: 「履いたまま」 = the state of having put them on. Since it's a noun, it connects like one: verbs and い-adjectives modify it directly, な-adjectives add 「な」, and nouns add 「の」. Followed by 「で」 or directly by a verb as an adverbial, it means “doing the next thing while keeping it as is”; followed by 「だ」 as a predicate, it means “has stayed as it was, hasn't changed”. The first verb is usually in the た-form, because what's being kept is a state that's already in place (left open, wearing, sitting), not an action in progress.

meaning: Means “without doing ... (and doing ... instead)”. It's the more formal, written-style version of 「〜ないで」.
connection: Verb ない-form minus ない + ずに (する → せずに, 来る → こずに)

senses.label: Without doing
senses.meaning: Doing the second action without doing the first: “without ...ing”. Same meaning as 「〜ないで」, but more formal.
senses.connection: Verb ない-stem + ずに (持たずに・使わずに・食べずに・せずに)
examples: I went out without an umbrella.
Please try reading it without a dictionary.
I went to school without eating breakfast.

senses.label: Instead of
senses.meaning: Not doing the first thing and doing the second instead: “instead of ..., ...”.
senses.connection: Verb ない-stem + ずに、〜 (バスに乗らずに歩く)
examples: Instead of taking the bus, I walked to the station.
Today I cooked at home instead of eating out.

senses.label: Still haven't
senses.meaning: 「〜ずにいる」 means you still haven't done (or haven't been able to do) something, and that state continues.
senses.connection: Verb ない-stem + ずにいる
examples: I still haven't been able to tell the truth.
I still can't remember his name.

notes: 「する」 must become 「せずに」: ✕「しずに」→ ○「せずに」 (「勉強せずに」); 「来る」 becomes 「こずに」.
「〜ずに」 can't be used for requests or prohibitions: ✕「触らずにください」→ ○「触らないでください」.
「〜ずに」 expresses manner or substitution, not a reason: ✕「雨が降らずに、困った」→ ○「雨が降らなくて、困った」 (I was in trouble because it didn't rain).
It sounds somewhat written; everyday speech mostly uses 「〜ないで」. But set phrases such as 「〜ずにはいられない」 require 「ず」.

etymology: 「ず」 is the negative auxiliary of classical Japanese, and 「に」 is a particle. 「〜ずに」 means “in a state of not ...”. It's a classical negative that survives in modern Japanese, which is why it sounds more formal than 「〜ないで」.

similar.title: 〜ないで (without doing)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: for “do ... without doing ...” it's interchangeable with 「〜ずに」, and 「〜ないで」 is more colloquial. Also, only 「〜ないで」 can take 「ください」: 「見ないでください」.

similar.title: 〜ことなく
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: 「〜ことなく」 also means “without ...”, but it's more formal and stronger than 「〜ずに」, often implying “not even once”: 「休むことなく働き続けた」.

similar.title: 〜ずに済む・〜ないで済む
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「〜ずに」 followed by 「済む」 means “got by without having to ...”, with a sense of relief: 「電車が動いていたので、タクシーに乗らずに済んだ」.

similar.title: 〜ずにはいられない
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「〜ずに」 followed by 「はいられない」, literally “can't stay without doing” → “can't help but ...”: 「笑わずにはいられない」. The meaning has shifted from “not doing” to “being compelled to do”.

formation: 「ず」 is the negative auxiliary of classical Japanese (the equivalent of modern 「ない」) and attaches to the verb's irrealis form (the nai-form minus 「ない」); 「に」 is a particle marking state or manner. 「〜ずに」 = “in a state of not doing ...”, modifying the following action to say it's done without doing the first one: 「傘を持たずに出かけた」. Because 「に」 only marks state or manner, it can't express a reason the way 「〜なくて」 does, and unlike the te-form 「〜ないで」 it can't take 「ください」 to make a request. The classical irrealis form of 「する」 is 「せ」, hence 「せずに」; its classical origin is also why it sounds more written than 「〜ないで」.

meaning: Uses the negative te-form to give a reason: “because ... not”, “because there's no ...”.
connection: Verb ない-form → 〜なくて; い-adjective → 〜くなくて; noun + が + なくて

senses.label: A negative reason
senses.meaning: Something didn't happen or isn't there, and that leads to the result. The second part is usually a state or outcome you can't control.
senses.connection: Verb ない-form → なくて (わからなくて・来なくて); noun が + なくて
examples: I didn't have time, so I couldn't eat breakfast.
I don't understand the homework, and I'm stuck.
The bus didn't come, so I was late.

senses.label: Reason for a feeling
senses.meaning: The second part is a word of feeling or judgment like 「残念」, 「心配」, 「すみません」 or 「よかった」, and 「〜なくて」 explains why you feel that way.
senses.connection: 〜なくて + 残念だ／心配した／すみません／よかった
examples: I'm sorry I couldn't help.
I'm so frustrated that I didn't pass the exam.
We didn't hear from you, so we were worried.

notes: The second clause can't be a command, request, intention or invitation: ✕「時間がなくて、タクシーで行きましょう」→ ○「時間がないので、タクシーで行きましょう」.
Mixing it up with 「〜ないで」 changes the meaning: for a reason, use 「〜なくて」 (✕「わからないで困った」→ ○「わからなくて困った」); for “did ... without doing ...”, use 「〜ないで」 (✕「朝ご飯を食べなくて学校へ行った」→ ○「食べないで学校へ行った」).
A spoken apology like 「行けなくて、すみません」 is perfectly natural, but in formal emails or to clients, the written 「〜ず」 is preferred: 「お役に立てず、申し訳ございません」.
「〜じゃなくて」 means “not A but B”, not a reason: 「学生じゃなくて、先生です」.

etymology: It's 「なくて」, the te-form of the negative auxiliary 「ない」. The te-form itself can mean “because ...”, so the negative 「なくて」 naturally means “because not ...”.

similar.title: 〜て・〜で (cause)
similar.explanation: Same origin: this pattern is simply the negative of 「〜て」 (cause). Affirmative: 「雨が降って、試合が中止になった」; negative: 「雨が降らなくて、野菜が育たない」. In neither can the second clause express an intention or request.

similar.title: 〜ないで (without doing)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning and the easiest to confuse: 「〜なくて」 gives a reason, 「〜ないで」 means “did ... without doing ...”: 「財布を持たないで出かけた」 (went out without my wallet) vs. 「財布がなくて困った」 (I was in trouble because I didn't have my wallet).

similar.title: 〜ので
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both express a reason. With 「〜ないので」 the cause-and-effect is explicit, and the second clause can be a request or intention: 「時間がないので、急いでください」; 「〜なくて」 can't do this.

formation: 「ない」 is a negative auxiliary that conjugates like an adjective, and its te-form is 「なくて」 (just like 「高い→高くて」). The te-form originally just links two events; when the first is a situation and the second a result that follows, it's naturally understood as a cause: 「時間がなくて、食べられなかった」. So 「〜なくて」 = “because (something) doesn't / there isn't ...”, and the second clause is usually an established fact, an uncontrollable result or a feeling. Since this causal meaning only comes out of simple sequencing, the cause-and-effect isn't as explicit as with 「ので」 or 「から」, which is why the second clause can't express the speaker's intention or a request.
